qt: to the Commission Emmanouil Fragkos (ECR) Subject:

Once again, Thessaloniki is drowning in rubbish, not to mention large amounts of litter on its pavements. This city, which aspires to play a key role in South-East Europe and attract high-quality tourism, is facing everyday problems that do it no credit. It is of particular concern that according to the European Air Quality Index1, Athens, Thessaloniki and Patras are permanently ‘red’, which highlights the systemic nature of the problem of cleanliness in Greece. European programmes such as TREASoURcE2, NeCOL3 and Zero Waste Cities4 have looked into the options for a modern waste collection system in cities, with due regard to resources and, of course, public health. Refuse collection is, of course, regarded as a national responsibility which is undertaken by municipalities and forms part of their internal organisation, but obviously there is scope for issuing guidance and for promoting good practice as well as assessing effectiveness, so that an additional incentive can be provided for achieving excellent results at European level. In view of this: 1.
How could the Commission help the city's administration access European best practices so that the urban cleanliness problems it faces can be dealt with effectively?
Is the Commission considering the possibility of assessing waste collection systems at local level?
Do Thessaloniki and other cities in Greece have access to underutilised European tools to allow their internal organisation to function more effectively?

(3 May 2024) The Commission has issued guidance to Member States, including best practices (5), on separate collection of waste to facilitate compliance with the requirements in EU law (6). In an early warning report (7), the Commission gave concrete recommendations to Greece to extend separate collection, implement economic instruments to incentivise it, and improve citizen awareness (8). The recommendations are based on assessments by the European Environment Agency which has also published informative analysis on tools to improve waste management (9). Under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (10) Greece has reformed its waste management policies by introducing incentives for municipalities to achieve higher recycling rates. At local level, Member States’ authorities are best placed to assess specific waste needs and develop collection systems. The Commission assessed such systems in the EU capitals (11). The Commission’s initiative ‘Green City Accord’ aims to improve the quality of life in cities and accelerate the implementation of EU environmental laws, including on circular economy and waste (12).

EU funding can support cities to better manage their waste, including through Cohesion Policy funds (13), subject to specific rules applicable to each tool (14). EU funding programmes are available to support cities in developing and implementing environmental action (15). The Circular City Funding Guide provides information on funding for circular economy initiatives and guidelines for setting up funding programmes (16). The EU has also supported initiatives such as the programme ‘Zero Waste Cities’, which helps cities and communities transition towards zero waste, bringing together a European platform of knowledge for local stakeholders to implement best practices (17).
